blogs.title: Same Similarity, Different Factor? The Federal Circuit Rejects a Narrower Lens for DuPont Factor Six
blogs.description: This post would analyze the opinion’s core doctrinal move: the court’s insistence that the TTAB cannot define service similarity broadly for DuPont factor two and then more narrowly for factor six. It would explore how Apex Bank v. CC Serve pushes toward greater internal consistency across likelihood-of-confusion factors, why the panel treated the Board’s narrowed “relevant public” as legal error rather than mere factfinding, and what this means for future attempts to cabin third-party-use evidence.

blogs.title: Crowded Fields and Weak Marks: What Apex Bank Means for Third-Party Use Evidence at the TTAB
blogs.description: This post would focus on the evidentiary implications of the remand. The court did not hold that ASPIRE is weak, but it made clear that third-party uses in adjacent financial-service categories may matter when the Board has already found those categories highly similar or partly legally identical. The post would situate the case alongside Juice Generation and Jack Wolfskin, examining whether the Federal Circuit is continuing to lower practical barriers to showing marketplace crowding and how applicants should build a stronger weakness record.

blogs.title: When ‘Credit Card Services’ Become ‘Banking and Financing Services’: Legacy Identifications and the Breadth of Trademark Rights
blogs.description: This post would examine the court’s affirmance on DuPont factor two, especially the Board’s treatment of an older registration for ‘credit card services’ after that entry disappeared from the ID Manual. It would discuss how the Board and court interpreted that legacy wording expansively, why that mattered in finding the parties’ services highly similar, and the broader consequences for owners of older registrations whose service descriptions may now sweep more broadly than modern drafting conventions would suggest.

blogs.title: A Partial Vacatur with Teeth: Why the Federal Circuit Sent the Mark-Similarity Analysis Back Too
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s decision to vacate not only factor six, but also factor one. The panel treated commercial strength and overall commercial impression as interconnected, suggesting that mark-similarity analysis cannot be cleanly separated from the crowded-field inquiry. The post would explore the significance of that linkage for TTAB adjudication, including whether boards and litigants should treat strength evidence as permeating multiple DuPont factors rather than being siloed in a single part of the analysis.
